domain.title: Website traffic
domain.summary: One week of visits to a website, counted every 10 minutes (1,008 values). The model says if the week looks normal or which kind of problem it has, and marks the moments that made it decide.
domain.data_note: The examples come from the WebTraffic test set (Early et al., ICLR 2024): made-up but realistic weekly traffic with one known problem added at a known place. The model never saw them while training.

classes.label: Normal
classes.description: A normal week: busy days, quiet nights and a weekly rhythm, with nothing odd added.

classes.label: Spikes
classes.description: Single values that jump far up or down and come straight back, like a glitch in the counter.

classes.label: Flipped part
classes.description: A part of 6 hours to 2 days is played backwards, so the daily pattern runs the wrong way.

classes.label: Time skew
classes.description: A part where time is squeezed on one side and stretched on the other, so the daily curve looks lopsided.

classes.label: Extra noise
classes.description: A part with much more random jitter than usual, for example from a broken sensor or logging problem.

classes.label: Outage
classes.description: Traffic suddenly falls to almost zero for a while, as if the site or the tracking went down.

classes.label: Too smooth
classes.description: A part that is too smooth - the usual small wiggles are gone, which can mean the data was filled in or estimated.

classes.label: Drift
classes.description: Traffic slowly moves away from its normal level over a while, then jumps back.

classes.label: Traffic peak
classes.description: A smooth bump of extra traffic on top of the normal pattern, like a campaign or a post going viral.

classes.label: Traffic dip
classes.description: A smooth dip where traffic is lower than it should be, like a partial outage or lost links.

model_card.architecture: SEA-Net: a small time-series model that is interpretable by design. The details of its design are private for now (research in progress).
model_card.how_it_explains: The model gives every single time step a score for every class, and its answer is built from those scores. Those per-step scores are what you see shaded on the chart - they are how the model decides, not something added afterwards.
model_card.baseline: MILLET (Early et al., ICLR 2024) trained on the same data: 91.6% test accuracy with 424K weights. MILLET does better on the deletion test (AOPCR); SEA-Net's evidence lands closer to the real problem (NDCG).
limitations: Trained only on made-up web-traffic weeks of 1,008 values. Real traffic that looks very different can get a confident but wrong answer.
Series shorter than 1,008 values are stretched first, which can blur very short events. Longer ones are cut into windows.
Each window is assumed to have at most one kind of problem.
